plan: [With three bidders the winner pays the third‑highest bid — i.e., the minimum of the three bids. My bid mostly only affects whether I win, not the price I pay. To maximize long‑run profit I should bid aggressively to win whenever at least one opponent is cheap. There is no history to exploit this round, and my value is $30, so I bid the maximum allowed to maximize expected surplus.]

[Opponents' bids unknown; assume symmetric increasing strategies and, as a tractable benchmark, that they bid their values (uniform on [0,49]). If opponents' bids are iid U(0,49), my win probability = (b/49)^2 and conditional payment ≈ b/3, so expected profit proportional to b^2(28 - b/3), which is increasing up to b=56. Constraint b≤49 => optimal bid at the upper bound. Bid the maximum allowed (49) to maximize expected surplus.]

[Three bidders, winner pays the lowest bid. Solving for a symmetric Bayes–Nash equilibrium using order statistics and the envelope condition yields b(v)=2v. This maximizes expected payoff given opponents use the same strategy. With independent uniform values on [0,49], bidding twice your value is optimal in equilibrium. For v=24, follow the equilibrium and bid 2*24=48.]
